overview.headline: Radioactive waste types, decay, storage and regulation basics

keyPoints.point: Waste has broad classifications for management.
keyPoints.quote: There are two broad classifications: high-level or low-level waste.

keyPoints.point: High-level waste uses spent fuel removed from reactors.
keyPoints.quote: High-level waste is primarily spent fuel removed from reactors after producing electricity.

keyPoints.point: Radioactivity will decay over time measured by half-lives.
keyPoints.quote: Strontium-90 and cesium-137 have half-lives of about 30 years (half the radioactivity will decay in 30 years).

keyPoints.point: Pools use reinforced concrete with steel liners for shielding.
keyPoints.quote: These pools are made of reinforced concrete several feet thick, with steel liners.

keyTerms.gloss: radioactive hazard remaining after long decay
keyTerms.quote: Transuranic wastes, sometimes called TRU, account for most of the radioactive hazard remaining in high-level waste after 1,000 years.

keyTerms.gloss: waste with broad classifications for near-surface disposal
keyTerms.quote: There are two broad classifications: high-level or low-level waste.

keyTerms.gloss: fuel removed from reactors after producing electricity
keyTerms.quote: High-level waste is primarily spent fuel removed from reactors after producing electricity.

keyTerms.gloss: isotopes that account for most heat and penetrating radiation
keyTerms.quote: These isotopes, called "fission products," account for most of the heat and penetrating radiation in high-level waste.

keyTerms.gloss: elements heavier than uranium that take longer to decay
keyTerms.quote: These heavier-than-uranium, or "transuranic," elements do not produce nearly the amount of heat

keyTerms.gloss: years needed for half the material to decay
keyTerms.quote: Plutonium-239 has a half-life of 24,000 years.
